input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

i am forwarding the packet with the photographs and the access sheet to mara this afternoon as the inspection record for the alder notch shed if the maintenance lead confirms that the handle pin on the second anchor is secure before the next scheduled group then jun can decide whether to return that anchor to the west rack otherwise it stays on the bench pending another check the orange harness also stays in the cabinet until jun checks its buckle report and carabiner c forty two remains tagged for review the condition notes describe what we saw on thursday and do not give a later check date mara can use the blank return visit field after the site contact sets one and the original shelf count is included so the next inspection can compare the same locations", "output": "I am forwarding the climbing gear inspection packet from the north wall shed to Mara Voss at the ridge office this afternoon. The packet covers the equipment check carried out on Thursday, April 11, at the Alder Notch training crag. Our crew included me, Lena Ortiz, and Caleb Finn, and the site contact was Jun Park. The inspection began at 8:10 in the morning after we signed the access sheet and checked the weather board. The board showed a low temperature of 38 degrees, a west wind, and a chance of light rain after noon. The rock stayed dry during our work, and the wind picked up only near the end.

The shed has two steel racks, a wooden bench, and a narrow cabinet for small hardware. The east rack holds team ropes and harnesses, and the west rack holds helmets, slings, carabiners, and the portable practice anchors. We counted the gear by shelf and wrote the shelf labels in the packet. The blue tag on the east rack reads “North wall team stock,” and the paper label on the cabinet says “Hardware awaiting review.” The cabinet latch did not close unless we lifted the door slightly, so we noted that for the site contact. Jun said, “The latch has done that since the thaw, and I will put it on the repair list.” The latch still stayed shut when we tested it gently after the inspection.

We checked the ropes on the bench one at a time and kept each rope separate from the next one. The first rope had a white sheath with a green thread marker and measured 40 meters. The second had a red sheath with a black marker and measured 35 meters, and the third was a shorter practice rope with a blue marker and measured 20 meters. Caleb read the maker and date labels while I looked for cuts, flat sections, and exposed core. Lena checked the rope ends and the sewn eyes. None of the three ropes had visible core, and we recorded their lengths as measured rather than relying on the faded tags. The white rope had a dark stain near one end, but the sheath was smooth across the stain, and it did not catch a fingernail.

Section 1: Harness review
1. The gray medium harness with the inventory number H-27. The waist buckle moved freely, and the leg loops held their adjustment during the test.
2. The orange small harness H-31. Its left leg loop buckle needed a second pull before it locked.
3. The blue large harness H-19. The label was creased, but the size and inventory number were still readable.

We checked each harness for torn stitching, damaged webbing, and unreadable labels, and wrote a separate note for every item. The orange harness remained in the cabinet rather than going back on the rack while Jun checked whether its buckle had been reported before.

We examined the helmets under the overhead light. The white helmet had a shallow scrape on the rim and no visible crack. The yellow helmet had a loose chin strap keeper, and we could slide the loose keeper along the strap with one finger. The red helmet had a faded date stamp that we could not read clearly, so we recorded it as unreadable instead of guessing. Each helmet had its own shelf mark, and we did not move the helmets into another group while we were checking them. Lena photographed the yellow helmet next to its shelf label for the inspection packet. Caleb wrote the photo time as 9:46 because the camera clock matched the wall clock to the minute.

On the west rack there were six sewn slings: three short black slings and three longer purple slings. We looked over each one for cuts, pulled threads, and damaged stitching, and then checked the labels. Two of the purple slings had labels that were difficult to read, but the dates remained legible. The carabiners were in a shallow tray below the slings. We counted 14 steel carabiners and eight aluminum carabiners, and opened and closed each gate once. One steel gate returned slowly after we released it. We tried it again without adding force and got the same result. Caleb marked that carabiner with a temporary orange tag and placed it in a separate corner of the tray. The tag said “Hold for review,” and he recorded its inventory number as C-42.

We took the portable practice anchors outside the shed and checked them on the flat gravel area near the trail map. The first anchor had two legs with worn paint near the feet but no visible bend. The second anchor had a loose handle pin that moved when Lena turned the handle by hand. We did not put weight on either anchor. Jun asked us to leave the second one on the bench until he could look at the pin with the maintenance lead. The first anchor went back beside the west rack after we recorded the condition and location. The access sheet required us to leave a clear path from the shed door to the trail, and we kept the bench and gravel area clear while making the notes.

The packet has a cover sheet, a shelf count, a rope page, a harness page, a helmet page, a sling and carabiner page, and two anchor notes. It also has four photographs with filenames and times. Caleb checked that each photograph had a matching description before we packed the pages. The inspection date on the cover sheet is April 11, and the return visit field is blank because the site contact had not set a date. Mara asked us by message to include the unclear helmet stamp and the item numbers for anything held aside. Her message said, “Please keep the condition notes beside the inventory number so I can compare them with the rack map.” We used that layout for the yellow helmet, the orange harness, and carabiner C-42.

Before leaving, we read the rack counts aloud while Jun compared them with the paper list. The team rope count was three, the harness count was three, the helmet count was three, the sling count was six, and the carabiner count was 22. The two anchors were both listed on the equipment sheet, though the second one stayed on the bench for the maintenance lead. Jun signed the access sheet at 10:32, and Lena wrote the time beside the shed key return. The key went into the numbered envelope in the wall box, and the envelope number was 12. No one changed the shelf labels during the inspection, and we left the temporary orange tag attached to C-42.

I am forwarding the packet with the photographs and the access sheet to Mara this afternoon as the inspection record for the Alder Notch shed. If the maintenance lead confirms that the handle pin on the second anchor is secure before the next scheduled group, then Jun can decide whether to return that anchor to the west rack; otherwise, it stays on the bench pending another check. The orange harness also stays in the cabinet until Jun checks its buckle report, and carabiner C-42 remains tagged for review. The condition notes describe what we saw on Thursday and do not give a later check date. Mara can use the blank return visit field after the site contact sets one, and the original shelf count is included so the next inspection can compare the same locations."}]
